summary:
Project Summary

The Balkan Wildfire Calendar is an interactive 3D geospatial platform designed to analyze 26 years (2000–2026) of wildfire activity across Southeastern Europe.

To address the challenge of sensor discrepancies between NASA’s historical MODIS (1 km resolution) and modern VIIRS (375 m resolution) thermal instruments, we engineered a high-speed pipeline harmonizing nearly one million hot spot records into a unified, high-performance database.

Recognizing that wildfires ignore administrative boundaries, the platform introduces a custom 3D drawing tool allowing users to define, manipulate, and query arbitrary geographic areas directly on a digital twin of Earth. Fire incidents are filtered via client-side ray-casting and aggregated into surface-flush 2D hexagonal density grids weighted by Fire Radiative Power (FRP). The interface also integrates monotonic, colorblind-safe palettes (Cividis and Viridis) to guarantee universal accessibility.

This platform bridges the gap between raw Earth observation data and regional disaster management, empowering cross-border emergency responders, environmental agencies, and climate researchers with rapid, accessible spatial intelligence.

Project Details: Balkan Wildfire Calendar

1. What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

The Balkan Wildfire Calendar is an interactive 3D geospatial analytics platform that harmonizes 959,664 NASA satellite hot spot records spanning from 2000 to 2026 across Southeastern Europe.

How it works step-by-step:

  1. High-Speed Ingestion & Harmonization: The backend ingested historical MODIS records and near-real-time VIIRS detections into a single PostgreSQL database via a high-speed binary COPY stream in under 8 seconds. Both sensor feeds are normalized into a unified spatial-temporal schema.
  2. Interactive 3D Digital Twin: Built on Globe.gl and Three.js with high-resolution ArcGIS satellite imagery, the application projects Earth as a high-fidelity 3D sphere.
  3. Custom Freeform Geographic Selection: Rather than restricting users to political borders, users can activate a custom drawing tool to place polygon vertices directly on the 3D globe surface. A mathematical raycaster converts 2D screen mouse clicks into spherical latitude/longitude coordinates (lat,lng)(\text{lat}, \text{lng})(lat,lng) in real time.
  4. Vertex Manipulation: Users can grab and drag any placed vertex point across the terrain to fine-tune geographic perimeters around specific valleys, national parks, or mountain ranges.
    • Server-Side: The backend queries a composite multi-column B-tree index on (Year, Month, Latitude, Longitude) using the polygon’s bounding box, retrieving candidate records in under 50 ms.
    • Client-Side: A ray-casting Point-in-Polygon (PIP) algorithm evaluates candidates against the exact polygon boundary, ensuring 100% of external fires are excluded.
  5. Flush 2D Hexagonal Binning: Detected fires are binned into surface-flush 2D hexagonal cells curved along Earth’s spherical ellipsoid. Cells are shaded based on density and weighted by Fire Radiative Power (FRP) in Megawatts.

2. What Benefits Does It Have?

  • Liberation from Administrative Boundaries: Users can analyze transnational wildfire corridors (such as the Dinaric Alps or Rhodope Mountains) without artificial border constraints.
  • Elimination of Visual Distortion: Traditional 3D fire maps rely on vertical bars or pillars that occlude background terrain and flare outward unnaturally on curved globes. Our 2D hexagonal outer layer sits flush on the surface (altitude: 0.0002), conforming smoothly to the Earth's sphere.
  • Lightning-Fast Responsiveness: By pairing database composite indexing with client-side PIP filtering, complex spatial queries across nearly 1,000,000 records return in milliseconds at 60 FPS.
  • Quantitative Energy Measurement: By analyzing Fire Radiative Power (FRP) alongside event counts, the platform distinguishes low-intensity agricultural burns from devastating high-energy crown wildfires.

3. What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

  • Cross-Border Emergency Response: Provides civil protection bodies (e.g., EU Civil Protection / rescEU) with instant, boundary-free situational reports for shared ecological zones.
  • Long-Term Climate & Ecological Research: Allows environmental scientists to evaluate 26-year historical fire regime trends without sensor-bias artifacts caused by the transition from MODIS to VIIRS.
  • Resource Allocation & Predictive Planning: Helps fire management authorities identify persistent multi-year mega-clusters and allocate firefighting aerial assets ahead of peak summer seasons.

4. Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

  • Backend: C#, ASP.NET Core 10, Entity Framework Core, Npgsql.
  • Database: PostgreSQL (hosted on Supabase) utilizing binary protocol streams and multi-column B-tree composite indexing.
  • 3D Visualization & Graphics: JavaScript (ES6+), Globe.gl, Three.js, CSS2DRenderer (for interactive vertex DOM handles), HTML5 Canvas.
  • Styling & UI: Tailwind CSS, Lucide Icons, Google Fonts (Inter, JetBrains Mono, Plus Jakarta Sans).
  • Data Sources: NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) harmonized MODIS (Terra/Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP/NOAA-20) datasets; ArcGIS World Imagery basemaps; Natural Earth topography; Balkan GeoJSON vector boundaries.

5. How Is Your Project Creative?

  • 3D Drafting on a Curved Sphere: Most GIS drawing tools are built for flat 2D maps (e.g., Leaflet or Mapbox). We engineered a vector drawing system directly on an orbiting 3D sphere, seamlessly decoupling camera controls during vertex dragging.
  • Curvature-Conforming 2D Hexagons: Instead of rendering hexagons as flat planes whose edges hover into space, our hexagons are tessellated with a curvature resolution of 8, wrapping smoothly around the planetary sphere like a glove.
  • Dynamic Harmonization: Rather than forcing disparate sensor resolutions into artificial grids, we aggregate unified thermal energy output (FRP) dynamically at runtime, creating a continuous historical visual narrative from 2000 to 2026.

6. Factors Considered by Our Team

  • Scientific Accessibility (Color-Vision Deficiency): Red-green color blindness affects roughly 8% of men. Standard red fire heatmaps appear muddy and unreadable to them. We integrated Cividis and Viridis palettes engineered with monotonic luminance, guaranteeing that "Darker = Denser" is universally readable across all human vision types.
  • Ecological Reality vs. Political Lines: Wildfires spread along fuel loads, winds, and topography, not national borders. Prioritizing custom polygon drawing was a deliberate design choice to reflect real-world fire behavior.
  • Performance & Bandwidth Optimization: Streaming nearly a million raw points directly to the browser would crash mobile devices and laptops. We engineered server-side bounding box pre-filtering and resolution-capped binning to keep client-side memory usage under 60 MB.

7. Future Developments

  • Weather Forecast Database Integration: Linking the platform with meteorological services and climate reanalysis databases (wind vector fields, relative humidity, surface temperature, and drought severity indexes) to correlate atmospheric drivers with wildfire spread and pinpoint historical anomalies.
  • AI & Machine Learning Predictive Modeling: Building and training machine learning models to detect longitudinal patterns, forecast emerging high-risk wildfire corridors, and automatically flag anomalous multi-year fire clusters across vulnerable Balkan biomes.
  • Advanced High-Resolution Surface Visualizer: Leveraging fine-grained geographical coordinates to develop an advanced vector shader/polygon engine that precisely contours, colors, and tracks the exact acreage of affected burn scars and perimeter boundaries.
  • Live NASA Real-Time Satellite Ingestion: Integrating automated streaming pipelines directly from NASA FIRMS Ultra Real-Time (URT) and Near Real-Time (NRT) satellite feeds, enabling civil protection authorities and researchers to visualize live wildfire hot spots within minutes of satellite overpass.
